rules.text: If the query image contains a distinct, localized structural change (e.g., a new building or cluster of buildings) that is clearly absent in the reference images, trust A (Agent).

If the visual difference between query and reference is a global texture or color shift across the entire field (e.g., plowing patterns or seasonal crop color) without a specific new object, trust A (Agent) to correctly identify this as normal.
If the query image shows a completely different scene or land use compared to the reference (e.g., undeveloped land vs. developed commercial area), trust B (Direct) to detect the anomaly.

If the query image contains small, bright, non-structural objects (e.g., swimming pools, tarps) that might be misclassified as building changes by A, trust B (Direct) to correctly label them as normal.
If the query image shows a large construction site or foundation that appears structurally similar to the surrounding residential pattern, trust B (Direct) to correctly identify it as normal.
Images exhibit a top-down aerial perspective with a granular, high-frequency texture representing ground surfaces.
The color palette is dominated by natural earth tones (browns, greens, greys) with no artificial neon or saturated hues.
Structures and terrain features display continuous, coherent boundaries without abrupt, unnatural geometric truncations.
Do not flag seasonal vegetation color changes (e.g., green to brown fields) or phenological shifts as building anomalies.
Ignore global image quality differences such as color casts, desaturation, or texture variations when no specific building structure is missing or added.
Do not classify natural landscape features like winding roads, ponds, or forest density variations as anomalies if they are consistent with the terrain.
